title: August and the Hymn
premise: Kestrel Amberdale hosts a late-night call-in show in the drowned valley town of Hallowmere, where the phones have started ringing with voices of listeners who died the week before. When an excavation crew unearths an iron door sealed from the inside beneath the old Amberdale chapel, Kestrel learns their family name is carved on it — and that the dead callers are counting down to the harvest moon, when whatever was locked in will be let out unless the last of the Amberdales are gone from town. As Kestrel's skepticism curdles into complicity — the station's ratings soar on grief, and the station owner wants the show never to stop — they must choose between the truth that destroys them and the lie that feeds the thing below. In the end, Kestrel goes on air one final time, tells every listener the truth about the door and the count, and walks into the chapel cellar as the moon rises, sealing the door from the inside themselves so the family line ends with them and the harvest goes unclaimed.
about_author: Emrys Eriksen is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent six years answering phones for shows no one admitted listening to. They write horror about small towns that keep secrets the way other towns keep time.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. During a routine broadcast of 'The Night Line,' a caller describes her own funeral from last Tuesday; Kestrel assumes a prank and cuts her off. The emotional beat is brittle professional detachment masking insomnia and dread, establishing Kestrel's refusal to believe anything they can't hold.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: Crew foreman Dov Hale's POV. The crew breaks ground behind the derelict Amberdale chapel and hits iron instead of stone: a door, hinges fused, sealed from the inside. Dov feels watched by the whole hillside. The beat is unease disguised as blue-collar bravado.

chapters.title: Second Caller
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A man calls asking Kestrel to apologize to his daughter for something only he knew; records confirm he drowned nine days ago. Kestrel pulls the call log and finds forty-one calls from the dead in two weeks. The beat is the first hairline crack in disbelief.

chapters.title: What the Door Says
chapters.summary: Dov's POV. Rubbing wax across the door reveals the name AMBERDALE carved deep, ringed by tally marks too many to count. That night his crew dreams of a hymn none of them know. The beat is inherited guilt arriving uninvited.

chapters.title: Ratings
chapters.summary: Station owner Marlowe Vetch's POV. Vetch discovers the dead-callers segment is the most-listened hour in county history and forbids Kestrel from investigating or mentioning it on air. The beat is corruption dressed up as opportunity, introducing power's seduction.

chapters.title: The Family Out Ahead of the Count
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. An elderly caller — dead thirty years — explains plainly: the door opens at the harvest moon, and every Amberdale must be out of Hallowmere before it does. Kestrel laughs, then checks the parish register and finds their own name already entered under 'deceased.' The beat is vertigo.

chapters.title: Sister Wren
chapters.summary: Wren Amberdale, Kestrel's estranged cousin and a lapsed deaconess, arrives in town uninvited, carrying their grandmother's hymnal. Her POV. She has known about the count since childhood and came to drag Kestrel out. The beat is loyalty offered as an ultimatum.

chapters.title: Hymn for the Under-Hill
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She plays the hymnal's final page for Kestrel: a harvest song whose verses are instructions, not worship — how to feed what waits, how to keep the count honest. Kestrel refuses to sing along. The beat is faith versus denial in one kitchen at 3 a.m.

chapters.title: Dov Breaks Protocol
chapters.summary: Dov's POV. Ordered by Vetch to keep digging, Dov's crew cracks the door's outer seal; nothing comes out, but every clock in camp stops at the same minute. One worker walks into the hill singing. The beat is the cost of obedience to money over sense.

chapters.title: The Show Must Go On
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Vetch rebrands the program 'Voices From Beyond' against Kestrel's protests; grieving families flood the lines, and Kestrel realizes they're now the town's medium whether they believe or not. The beat is complicity — Kestrel keeps broadcasting because stopping would mean admitting it's real.

chapters.title: Tally
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She counts the marks on the door and matches them to the hymnal: each mark is a soul fed, and the count is nearly full. The missing marks correspond to living Amberdales. The beat is arithmetic becoming horror — the family isn't fleeing the door; it's being collected.

chapters.title: Vetch's Bargain
chapters.summary: Vetch's POV. He meets something in the station basement after hours — a voice on a dead line offering him the biggest signal in three counties if the show never stops and the Ambers stay in town. He says yes. The beat is power accepting its price without blinking.

chapters.title: Roadblock
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Wren try to leave town ahead of schedule; every road loops back to Hallowmere, gas gauges refilling themselves. A patrolman who died in spring waves them through with a smile. The beat is claustrophobia — the count won't release its own.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Tape
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. In the chapel attic they find a reel-to-reel: their grandmother broadcasting this same show in 1961, taking calls from the dead, ending mid-sentence as the moon rose. The tape ends with her walking downstairs toward the door. The beat is inheritance as sentence.

chapters.title: The Missing Verse
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Comparing the hymnal to the tape, she finds a verse torn out — the one that closes the count instead of feeding it. It requires an Amberdale to sing it inside the threshold, willingly, at moonrise. The beat is hope arriving shaped like sacrifice.

chapters.title: Silenced
chapters.summary: Vetch's POV. He fires Kestrel, locks the studio, and prepares to host the final broadcast himself with a voice that isn't quite his anymore. Meanwhile the dead callers go quiet — all of them at once. The beat is the machinery of exploitation turning on its operator.

chapters.title: Breaking In
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Wren break into their own station through the transmitter shed while the town sleeps standing up in its yards, faces turned to the rising moon. The beat is urgency sharpened into resolve; loyalty finally pointed at truth instead of survival.

chapters.title: On Air
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. They seize the board and tell every listener everything: the door, the count, the lie Vetch sold. The dead call in not to haunt but to say goodbye, one by one, freeing the town's grief. The beat is confession as weapon — truth breaking the spell of silence.

chapters.title: The Chapel Cellar
chapters.summary: Dov's POV. Dov, half-hollowed by the hymn, holds the door's outer seal open long enough for Kestrel to descend; Vetch follows, screaming about his signal, and the dark takes him first. The beat is a minor character choosing redemption at the threshold.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Below, Kestrel sees what the count was for — a patient, patient hunger wearing generations of Amberdale faces — and begins the missing verse as the moonlight reaches the cellar stairs. The beat is terror transfigured into purpose.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. From above, Wren hears the hymn finish and the door swing shut on its own, fusing like it had never been opened. The tally marks smooth to blank iron. The beat is grief and relief indivisible — the family saved by its ending.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, weeks later. She takes over the Night Line; the phones are just phones now, mostly. On her last night, one call comes through — Kestrel's voice, calm, saying only 'count's closed' before the dial tone. The beat is haunted peace: some doors you don't knock on again.
